strings.factoid_001: The first widely-recognized emoji set — 176 icons — was designed in 1998–99 by Shigetaka Kurita, then 25, for Japanese carrier NTT DoCoMo's mobile internet platform.
strings.factoid_002: Each original Kurita emoji was drawn on a grid of just 12×12 pixels — 144 dots total.
strings.factoid_003: Kurita's complete 176-icon set took up roughly 3 kilobytes of data.
strings.factoid_004: The word "emoji" comes from Japanese e (picture) + moji (character) — it's not actually derived from the English word "emotion," despite the coincidental resemblance.
strings.factoid_005: Kurita drew on manga, weather symbols, and the Zapf Dingbats typeface as visual inspiration for his original icons.
strings.factoid_006: Kurita said the 144-pixel grid was especially hard to work with because it had no true center point, which made symmetrical designs difficult.
strings.factoid_007: In 2016 the Museum of Modern Art in New York acquired Kurita's original 176 emoji as a gift from NTT DoCoMo, putting them in its permanent design collection.
strings.factoid_008: Emoji stayed almost entirely confined to Japanese phone networks for over a decade before going global.
strings.factoid_009: Emoji were folded into the official Unicode Standard starting with version 6.0 in 2010, which is what let the same characters render (if not look identical) across different phone brands.
strings.factoid_010: Apple built a hidden emoji keyboard into the original iPhone specifically to compete for the Japanese market — it wasn't meant for a global audience at first, but curious users elsewhere found ways to unlock it.
strings.factoid_011: Apple didn't officially open the emoji keyboard to all iOS users outside Japan until iOS 5 in 2011.
strings.factoid_012: The red heart emoji (❤️) has a claim to being one of the very first emoji ever made — it started life as a heart pictogram on an NTT DoCoMo pager aimed at teens, predating the full 176-icon set.
strings.factoid_013: Kurita's emoji were an instant hit in Japan and were quickly copied by rival Japanese phone carriers.
strings.factoid_014: Kurita later went to work for the Japanese gaming company Dwango.
strings.factoid_015: New emoji aren't added by any single tech company — they go through the nonprofit Unicode Consortium, whose voting members include Apple, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and Samsung.
strings.factoid_016: Anyone — not just companies — can write and submit a formal emoji proposal to Unicode's Emoji Subcommittee.
strings.factoid_017: A serious emoji proposal has to argue its case with evidence — things like Google Trends data, expected frequency of use, and why the concept isn't already covered by an existing emoji.
strings.factoid_018: The Unicode Emoji Subcommittee wasn't formally established until 2015, even though emoji had already been part of the Unicode Standard for five years.
strings.factoid_019: Getting from an accepted proposal to an emoji actually appearing on your phone typically takes a year or more, since it also has to be designed and shipped by every vendor.
strings.factoid_020: Unicode has been deliberately approving fewer new emoji each year since the mid-2010s; 2022's batch (Emoji 15.0) was the smallest since the standardized annual process began.
strings.factoid_021: Unicode has said it will no longer accept new proposals for country/region flag emoji (🏳️) at all, citing low usage relative to other categories.
strings.factoid_022: Because Unicode only defines an emoji's meaning and reference sketch, not its final look, the same emoji can appear as a completely different drawing depending on whether you're using an iPhone, an Android phone, or Windows.
strings.factoid_023: A 15-year-old Saudi high-school student, Rayouf Alhumedhi, wrote and championed the proposal that became the "Person with Headscarf" emoji (🧕), after finding no emoji represented her hijab.
strings.factoid_024: Alhumedhi's hijab-emoji (🧕) proposal cited roughly 550 million Muslim women worldwide who wear a hijab as part of the case for why the emoji keyboard needed one.
strings.factoid_025: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian publicly backed Alhumedhi's hijab-emoji (🧕) campaign.
strings.factoid_026: The hijab emoji's (🧕) beige color was reportedly chosen deliberately as a culturally neutral shade rather than tying it to one skin tone.
strings.factoid_027: The hijab emoji (🧕) went from proposal to shipping on devices in under a year, launching on World Emoji Day 2017.
strings.factoid_028: Not everyone welcomed the hijab emoji (🧕) — some social media reactions framed it as endorsing an oppressive symbol, a criticism Alhumedhi pushed back on directly.
strings.factoid_029: JoyPixels, an emoji vendor, says it successfully got a mermaid emoji (🧜‍♀️) added to Unicode by proposing that its cultural staying power justified inclusion.
strings.factoid_030: Emoji skin-tone modifiers (👋🏻👋🏽👋🏿) weren't added until 2015, as part of Unicode 8.0.
strings.factoid_031: The five skin-tone options (🏻🏼🏽🏾🏿) are based on the Fitzpatrick scale, a six-category dermatology tool created in 1975 to gauge how skin reacts to UV light — not a scale invented for emoji at all.
strings.factoid_032: In the Fitzpatrick-based emoji palette, dermatology's Types I and II are merged into a single "light" option (🏻), while Types III through VI each get their own emoji tone.
strings.factoid_033: Before 2015, Unicode's guidance was that human emoji should look "as neutral as possible" regarding race and gender — the plain yellow face (🙂) was meant as that neutral default.
strings.factoid_034: Combining a base emoji with a skin-tone modifier and a gender symbol via an invisible "zero width joiner" character is how a single emoji like "woman lifting weights with a specific skin tone" (🏋️‍♀️🏽) actually gets built behind the scenes.
strings.factoid_035: In August 2016, Apple replaced its black revolver-style gun emoji with a bright green toy water pistol (🔫).
strings.factoid_036: Apple also lobbied against — and helped block — a proposed realistic rifle emoji from ever being added to Unicode at all.
strings.factoid_037: Google held out the longest among major platforms, only switching its gun emoji (🔫) to a water gun in 2018, well after Apple, Twitter, and Samsung had already made the change.
strings.factoid_038: When Facebook and WhatsApp switched their gun emoji (🔫) to a water pistol, Microsoft was actually moving the opposite direction, swapping its cartoonish ray-gun icon for a more realistic-looking revolver.
strings.factoid_039: A French court ruled that sending a gun emoji (🔫) could constitute a death threat, sentencing a man to three months in prison for texting it to his ex-girlfriend.
strings.factoid_040: A 12-year-old in Virginia was charged after allegedly threatening her school in a social media post that combined gun, knife, and bomb emoji (🔫🔪💣).
strings.factoid_041: An advocacy campaign called #DisarmTheiPhone, run by the group New Yorkers Against Gun Violence, lobbied Apple for roughly a year before the company agreed to drop the realistic gun emoji (🔫).
strings.factoid_042: In 2023, a Saskatchewan court ruled that a farmer's thumbs-up emoji (👍), sent in reply to a photographed contract, legally counted as his signature accepting an $82,000 flax deal.
strings.factoid_043: The judge in that case pointed to the parties' history of confirming past deals with equally short texts like "ok" and "looks good" as evidence the thumbs-up (👍) carried real contractual weight.
strings.factoid_044: Saskatchewan's Court of Appeal upheld the thumbs-up (👍) ruling in a split decision — one dissenting judge argued a true signature should require something more deliberate than a single tapped emoji.
strings.factoid_045: The losing party in that case later asked Canada's Supreme Court to weigh in on whether an emoji (👍) can count as a legally binding signature.
strings.factoid_046: Oxford Dictionaries named the "Face with Tears of Joy" emoji (😂) its 2015 Word of the Year — the first time in the award's history that a non-word pictograph won.
strings.factoid_047: That emoji (😂) made up about 20% of all emoji used in the UK and 17% in the US in 2015, based on keyboard-app data Oxford analyzed with SwiftKey.
strings.factoid_048: That was a sharp jump from the same emoji's (😂) 4% (UK) and 9% (US) usage share just a year earlier, in 2014.
strings.factoid_049: Oxford's official 2015 write-up noted that overall usage of the word "emoji" in English more than tripled that year.
strings.factoid_050: Despite crowning an emoji Word of the Year, Oxford said at the time it had no plans to actually add emoji characters into its dictionary entries.
strings.factoid_051: According to Unicode Consortium data reported by the New York Times, "Face with Tears of Joy" (😂) was the single most-used emoji worldwide in 2021, with the red heart (❤️) in second place.
strings.factoid_052: In that same 2021 dataset, nine of the ten most-used emoji were unchanged from Unicode's previous ranking in 2019.
strings.factoid_053: The syringe emoji's (💉) popularity ranking jumped from 282nd place in 2019 to 193rd in 2021 — a shift researchers linked to COVID-19 vaccination messaging.
strings.factoid_054: By Emojipedia's 2023 tally of tweets, "Face with Tears of Joy" (😂) was still the world's #1 most-used emoji, followed by "Rolling on the Floor Laughing" (🤣) and the red heart (❤️).
strings.factoid_055: More recent tracking suggests the "Loudly Crying Face" emoji (😭) has since overtaken the laughing emoji (😂) in raw usage volume on some platforms, partly because Gen Z uses it to signal something is funny, not just sad.
strings.factoid_056: Emoji popularity varies a lot by platform: the red heart (❤️) tends to dominate on YouTube, the star emoji (⭐) is especially popular on China's Weibo, and skull and fire emoji (💀🔥) are common on Twitch.
strings.factoid_057: During the early COVID-19 pandemic, Emojipedia found that positive smiley-face emoji (🙂) usage actually declined slightly, even as overall emoji use kept climbing.
strings.factoid_058: Face with Tears of Joy (😂) is the most common top emoji in 75 different countries, according to Twitter data mapped by Vivid Maps.
strings.factoid_059: The red heart emoji (❤️) is the single most-used emoji in 18 different European countries, per the same Twitter dataset.
strings.factoid_060: Antigua and Barbuda was found to be the only country worldwide where the "Loudly Crying Face" emoji (😭), rather than laughing or heart emoji, ranks as the single most popular.
strings.factoid_061: Nigeria and Ghana were both found to favor "Face with Tears of Joy" (😂) as their top emoji, the same as the US, UK, and Canada.
strings.factoid_062: World Emoji Day (📅), celebrated every July 17, was invented in 2014 by Jeremy Burge, the founder of the emoji-reference site Emojipedia.
strings.factoid_063: The date July 17 was picked purely because Apple's calendar emoji (📅), as an Easter egg, displayed "July 17" on its little calendar page — a nod to when Apple's iCal software debuted at Macworld in 2002.
strings.factoid_064: Once World Emoji Day caught on, other companies' calendar emoji (📅) — including Samsung's, Google's, Twitter's, and JoyPixels's — were redesigned to also show July 17, to match Apple's.
strings.factoid_065: Since 2017, Apple has used World Emoji Day (📅 July 17) as its regular annual date for rolling out that year's new emoji designs.
strings.factoid_066: Emojipedia now runs an annual "World Emoji Awards" (🏆) on World Emoji Day, letting the public vote for things like most anticipated new emoji.
strings.factoid_067: Sony's 2017 animated feature "The Emoji Movie" (🎬) is one of the worst-reviewed wide theatrical releases in Rotten Tomatoes history, scoring in the single digits, yet it still grossed about $218 million worldwide against a $50 million budget.
strings.factoid_068: Sony's own marketing chief argued the film's under-8% critic score didn't hurt ticket sales because it opened in line with pre-release tracking and pulled an A-minus audience grade from young viewers.
strings.factoid_069: In 2015, Domino's became the first major brand to let customers place and complete an order just by tweeting the pizza-slice emoji (🍕) at its Twitter account.
strings.factoid_070: Domino's emoji-ordering (🍕) system worked by matching the sender's Twitter handle to a pre-saved "Easy Order" on file, then confirming by direct message.
strings.factoid_071: Early testers of Domino's emoji-ordering (🍕) feature found the onboarding setup more cumbersome than the "just tweet an emoji" pitch implied.
strings.factoid_072: "Emoji Dick" (🐳), a full crowdsourced translation of Herman Melville's "Moby-Dick" into emoji, was funded through an $3,500 Kickstarter campaign in 2009.
strings.factoid_073: Each of the roughly 10,000 sentences in Emoji Dick (🐳) was independently translated three separate times by different Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, and the most popular version of each sentence was voted into the final book.
strings.factoid_074: Over 800 crowdworkers collectively spent close to 3.8 million seconds — more than 1,000 hours — translating "Moby-Dick" into emoji (🐳) for that project.
strings.factoid_075: In 2013, the Library of Congress formally added Emoji Dick (🐳) to its catalog, making it (by most accounts) the first book written in emoji to enter the collection.
strings.factoid_076: Its creator, Fred Benenson, has said only about one in ten sentences in Emoji Dick (🐳) genuinely land as a clever "translation" rather than a garbled string of pictures.
strings.factoid_077: Jennifer Daniel, chair of Unicode's Emoji Subcommittee (and a Google designer), has said the group deliberately wants the emoji keyboard to avoid feeling like a cluttered "junk drawer" of one-off symbols.
strings.factoid_078: Real-world evidence of how an emoji is already being used informally — for example, the ring emoji (💍) showing up heavily in wedding-related posts — has directly influenced which related emoji, like a bride (👰), later got approved.
strings.factoid_079: Unicode Technical Report #51 is the formal specification document that lays out exactly how emoji proposals are evaluated, including criteria like "frequency of use" and "distinctiveness" from existing emoji.
strings.factoid_080: Emoji researchers Miltner and colleagues have argued that the mostly-white composition of Unicode's early decision-making committees shaped how "sensitive" the group considered questions of racial representation in emoji design.
strings.factoid_081: According to a 2025 Brandwatch consumer survey, 81% of Americans reported having felt confused by someone else's emoji usage.
strings.factoid_082: That same survey found 48% of respondents had personally witnessed an awkward situation caused by a misread emoji.
strings.factoid_083: Survey data cited by Brandwatch found female respondents aged 18–24 used the "Loudly Crying Face" emoji (😭) far more than male respondents in the same age group, who leaned toward fire and laughing-face emoji (🔥😂) instead.
strings.factoid_084: In China, the clapping-hands emoji (👏) doesn't primarily mean applause the way it does in much of the English-speaking world — a reminder that emoji meaning isn't actually a universal language.
strings.factoid_085: Unicode's own naming for the light skin-tone emoji modifier (🏻) is the somewhat clinical "Emoji Modifier Fitzpatrick Type-1-2."
strings.factoid_086: Zero-width joiner (ZWJ) sequences — invisible connector characters — are the technical trick that lets multiple separate emoji, like a person, a heart, and another person, be strung together and rendered as a single combined "family" or "couple" emoji (👨‍❤️‍👨).
strings.factoid_087: World Emoji Day's (📅) official Twitter/X account posted its very first #WorldEmojiDay tweet on July 11, 2014, several days before the first actual celebration.
strings.factoid_088: Before World Emoji Day existed as an organized event, some people already had a habit of informally posting the calendar emoji (📅) on July 17 each year, just because of the date shown on it.
strings.factoid_089: The London Royal Opera House once staged a season promotion built around describing operas and ballets purely through strings of emoji (🎭).
strings.factoid_090: Rayouf Alhumedhi originally worked around not having a hijab emoji by combining the existing "Man with Turban" (👳) and "Woman" (👩) emoji with an arrow between them.
strings.factoid_091: The hijab emoji's (🧕) official Unicode name is "Person with Headscarf," not "hijab emoji" — a wording choice partly meant to keep the character broadly usable rather than tying it to one specific religious garment.
strings.factoid_092: Two positive design factors Unicode weighs heavily in emoji proposals are how often a concept is already used and whether that same emoji could plausibly be used for more than one meaning (used metaphorically, not just literally).
strings.factoid_093: Once a Unicode Technical Committee approves an emoji, it can still take another six to twelve months (or longer) before individual companies finish designing, testing, and shipping their own version of it.
strings.factoid_094: As of a 2024 count, the Unicode Technical Committee itself had nine full voting member organizations deciding the fate of new emoji proposals.
strings.factoid_095: A recent count found Unicode 17.0 (released roughly September 2025) added only about eight new emoji, including a trombone (🎺) and an orca (🐋) — a sign of how selective the yearly additions have become.
strings.factoid_096: Since 2021, Unicode has run its emoji-proposal submission window only once a year, open from April 15 through August 31.
strings.factoid_097: That annual submission-window system replaced a rolling, less structured process, and was introduced partly in response to a COVID-related six-month delay to a Unicode release.
strings.factoid_098: In early 2016, Unicode's public "candidate" list for a future release already included dozens of emoji still pending — 74 candidates for one version alone, on top of newer ones proposed for the version after that — showing just how much of a backlog builds up before anything ships.
strings.factoid_099: Emojipedia gives out a "Lifetime Achievement Award" (🏆) as part of its annual World Emoji Awards — in 2023, on the awards' 10th anniversary, it went to the "Rolling on the Floor Laughing" emoji (🤣).
strings.factoid_100: In that 2023 Emojipedia analysis, 26.71% of all tweets sampled contained at least one emoji — described at the time as a record high.
